country.comment: The study examines Brazilian federalism and basic sanitation policy across Brazil's federal government, states/Federative Units, and municipalities.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Resumo, and Abstract; PDF pp. 5-10, Section 3

effect_estimate.comment: No inferential statistical model or causal point estimate is reported; the study synthesizes legal-institutional analysis with descriptive administrative indicators from SNIS (2017), Ministry of Cities (2017), SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, and SIOP (2020).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Descriptive legal-institutional analysis finds that dispersion of federal sanitation actions across multiple agencies with uncoordinated territorial mandates, asymmetric decentralization without adequate fiscal transfers or technical assistance, audit/control penalties, and high collective network maintenance costs inhibit municipal implementation—especially in municipalities under 50,000 inhabitants—perpetuating vertical inequality in sanitation access: in 2017, only 5 Federative Units had >50% of households with treated sewage (while in 4 states coverage was <10%), only 43% of 3,905 surveyed municipalities had a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan (>60.0% in municipalities >100,000 inhabitants, prompting 4 federal decree deadline postponements), and about 30% of 5,570 municipalities participated in public sanitation consortia.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumo and Abstract; PDF pp. 6-9, Section 3 (Gráficos 1-3, Figura 1); PDF pp. 11-12, Section 4 (Gráfico 4)

mechanism_certainty.comment: Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (design ceiling = 2). Coded as 1 because official secondary datasets and federal decrees document descriptive associations between municipal population size, planning/consortium instruments, federal program fragmentation, declining budgets, and low sanitation coverage, whereas the causal operation of federative/administrative barriers on household access is synthesized from secondary reports rather than directly observed through primary fieldwork.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6-9, Section 3 (Gráficos 1-3, Figura 1); PDF pp. 11-13, Section 4 (Gráfico 4)

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines Municipal and State Basic Sanitation Plans and 4 statutory deadline postponements (planning); regulatory criteria for federal funding, environmental licensing, and procurement bottlenecks (procedural_steps); implementing-agency and budgetary discretion (discretion); penalization/oversight by audit and control bodies such as TCU (sanction); municipal councils and social control mechanisms (participation); dispersion of federal sanitation programs across multiple ministries/agencies with separate territorial mandates (institutional_fragmentation); vertical/horizontal federative coordination and intermunicipal public consortia (political_coordination); and federal technical assistance and municipal capacity-building deficits (bureaucratic_assistance).

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes deficits and vertical/regional inequalities in access to basic sanitation and treated sewage networks (sanitation_access), household sewage network coverage percentages across Brazilian Federative Units (service_coverage), and statutory/PLANSAB targets for water supply and good-quality water provision alongside sanitation (water_access).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: The study combines constitutional/legislative doctrinal analysis of Brazilian sanitation and federalism laws with descriptive institutional evidence from official federal administrative and budgetary databases, fitting the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework rather than the six conventional epidemiological/qualitative tools or AMSTAR 2.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumo and Abstract; PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1; PDF pp. 5-13, Sections 3-4

sample_size.comment: No primary empirical sample size or sampling frame is reported; the study is a legal-institutional policy analysis that cites descriptive secondary figures from official databases, including 3,905 surveyed municipalities in the 2017 Ministry of Cities Panorama dos Planos de Saneamento Básico, 5,570 municipalities and Brazil's Federative Units in SNIS (2017), SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN federal program counts, and 2015-2019 SIOP federal budget execution records.
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1; PDF pp. 6-9, Section 3; PDF pp. 11-12, Section 4

study_design.comment: Non-systematic literature review paired with analysis of federal constitutional/statutory sanitation norms and descriptive secondary data from official government databases (SNIS, Ministry of Cities, SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, SIOP) and TCU audit reports.
study_design.value: Legal-institutional and policy analysis combining narrative literature review, doctrinal/legislative analysis, and descriptive analysis of official federal administrative and budgetary databases
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumo and Abstract; PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1
